opening: The path to the lighthouse runs along the top of the point, between low grass and grey stone. It is late in the evening, and the light has almost gone from the sky. Out to your left, the sea is calm and dark, moving slowly against the rocks below. Ahead of you, at the very end of the land, the tower stands white and tall, and beside it there is a small stone cottage with one warm window.

The keeper has gone ashore for the night, to visit his sister in the town across the bay. He left you a note on the cottage door, held in place by a small brass pin. It says, in neat, careful handwriting: The kettle is filled. The lamp is ready. There is nothing to worry about. The sea is kind tonight.

You open the door. Inside, the cottage is small and quiet and warm. There is a stove in the corner with a low fire still glowing in it, and a wooden table by the window, and a rocking chair with a folded blanket over its arm. The walls are whitewashed, and on a shelf by the door there is a row of old blue jugs, and a jar of matches, and a small brass bell.
Close the door behind you. Hang your coat on the hook. Let your shoulders come down a little, now that you are inside.

Through the window, you can hear the sea. It is not loud. It is a slow, steady sound, like someone breathing in their sleep. A wave comes in over the stones, and settles, and draws back. And then another. And then another. There is no hurry in it at all.

The station is almost empty now. A porter wheels the last trolley past the lamps, and somewhere up ahead the engine lets out a long, patient breath of steam. You step up into the carriage, and the door closes softly behind you.

Your compartment is small and warm. The walls are panelled in old walnut, polished by a hundred years of hands, and a brass lamp glows on the wall beside your seat. Its light is low and amber, the colour of honey held up to a candle. There is a deep red armchair, a wool blanket folded over its arm, and a little table by the window with a cup of something hot waiting for you.
Sit down. Let the chair take your weight.

Outside, a whistle sounds, far off and gentle. The carriage gives a small, polite jolt, and then, so slowly you almost miss it, the platform begins to slide away. The station lamps drift past the window one by one. Then the last of them is gone, and there is only the dark, and the sound of the wheels.

Listen to them for a moment. Each wheel meets the joint in the rail, and lets it go. Meets it, and lets it go. It is the oldest rhythm there is on a railway, and it asks nothing of you. You do not have to count it. You do not have to keep up. The train will keep the time tonight.

Draw the blanket over your knees. Feel the weight of it settle, warm and heavy, the way snow settles on a roof. Your hands can rest on top of it. Your shoulders can come down a little, and then a little more.

The pier is quiet at this hour. A single lamp hangs from a post at the end of it, and a few moths drift slowly through its light. The ferry waits beside the boards, low and broad and painted white, its windows glowing a soft yellow. A deckhand in a wool sweater nods to you and lifts the rope from the post. You step across the narrow gap, and the deck takes your weight with a small, friendly dip.

Inside, the cabin is long and low, with a ceiling of pale painted boards. There are wooden benches with deep cushions, and a little iron stove in the corner, burning low. Your berth is at the far end, by a round window. The bed is made up with clean white sheets and a heavy quilt the colour of oatmeal. A small lamp is fixed to the wall above the pillow, under a green glass shade.
Sit on the edge of the bed. Take off your shoes. Let your feet rest on the warm boards.

Somewhere below you, the engine wakes. It does not roar. It turns over once, twice, and then settles into a low, even hum that you feel more than hear. It comes up through the floor and into the soles of your feet. The ferry eases away from the pier, so gently that the only sign is the lamp on the post, sliding slowly backwards past the window, and then gone.
Now there is only the water.

Listen to it. It comes along the side of the hull in small waves, one after another. Each one rises, touches the wood, and falls away. Rises, and falls away. There is no hurry in it. The lake has been doing this all night, and it will keep doing it long after you are asleep. You do not need to listen closely. It will go on whether you listen or not.

text: You have woken in the night. That is all right. It happens to everyone, and it does not mean the night is lost. There is still plenty of time to rest.
You do not need to check the time. You do not need to work anything out. Just stay where you are, warm and still, and let me help you find your way back.
Let your eyes close again.
Notice the bed beneath you. The weight of the blanket. The cool of the pillow against your cheek. You are safe, and warm, and there is nothing you need to do.
Let's slow the breath down together. Breathe in gently, through your nose, for a count of four. One... two... three... four.
And breathe out, slowly, for a count of six. One... two... three... four... five... six.
Again. In... two... three... four.
And out... two... three... four... five... six.
Keep breathing like this, at your own pace. A gentle breath in. A long, slow breath out. Each breath out tells your body that it is safe to rest.

If your mind has started to wander into tomorrow, that is all right too. Thoughts that come at night always feel bigger than they really are. They will be smaller in the morning. You can leave them there for now.
Let your face soften. Let your jaw loosen. Let your shoulders sink back into the bed.
Let your arms grow heavy. Let your legs grow heavy. Let your whole body sink a little deeper into the warm dark.
Now, very slowly, count backwards with me, from ten. With each number, let yourself sink a little further down. As if you were walking slowly down a soft staircase, into a deeper, quieter room.
Ten.
Nine.
Eight. A little deeper.
Seven.
Six. Heavier, and warmer.
Five.
Four. Further down.
Three.
Two. Almost there.
One.
You are at the bottom of the stairs now, in a quiet, dark, warm room. There is nowhere else you need to go.
If you are still awake, that is fine. Simply rest here. Resting is still good for you. Sleep will come back when it is ready.
A gentle breath in. A long, slow breath out.
Let the night carry you the rest of the way.
Get comfortable, and let your head sink into the pillow. Let the bed hold you. The day is over now, even if your mind has not quite noticed yet.
If your thoughts are busy tonight, that is all right. A busy mind is not a problem to be solved. It is simply a mind that has been working hard, and has not yet been told that it can stop.
So for a little while, we will let the day go, one piece at a time.
Close your eyes.
Breathe in slowly. And breathe out, a little longer than you breathed in. As if you were letting air out of a balloon, gently, steadily.
Again. In. And a long, slow breath out.
Now picture a small stream, running quietly through a wood at dusk. The water is clear and unhurried. Leaves drift down from the trees and land on its surface, and the water carries them away.
Each time a thought comes to you, of something you did today, or something you have to do tomorrow, imagine placing it on a leaf. Set it gently on the water. And watch it drift away downstream.
You do not have to push it. You do not have to follow it. The stream will carry it. That is what streams are for.
Another thought. Another leaf. Set it down. Let it go.
Perhaps a worry comes. Something unfinished. You can place that on a leaf too. It will still be there in the morning, if it needs to be. But it does not need you tonight.
Notice how the stream keeps moving. It never holds on to anything for long. Leaf after leaf, it carries them all, quietly, out of sight.
Now let the stream fade a little, and come back to your breath. Breathe in. And a long breath out.
Think of one small thing from today that was good. It does not have to be important. A warm drink. A kind word. A moment of quiet. Let yourself remember it.
Hold it for a moment, like something warm in your hands. Then let that go too, gently. You can keep the feeling, and let the rest drift away.
Now there is very little left to think about. The stream is quiet. The wood is dark and still. The leaves have all floated away.
Let your thoughts grow slower. Softer. Further apart. Like the last few leaves, drifting down, one at a time.
If another thought appears, that is fine. Set it on the water. Let it go. And come back to the quiet.
The day is finished. You did enough. You can rest now.
Breathe in. And let it all go.
Sleep well.
Settle into bed, and let yourself get comfortable. Move a little if you need to, until your body feels supported, the pillow under your head, the blanket over you.

For the next few minutes, we will travel slowly through the body, from the top of your head to the tips of your toes, and let each part soften as we go. You do not need to do anything well. You only need to notice, and let go.
Let your eyes close, whenever you are ready.
Take a slow breath in through your nose. And let it out, gently, through your mouth, as if you were sighing at the end of a long day.
And once more. Breathe in. And let it go.
Now let your breathing find its own pace. You do not need to control it. Just let it come and go, like the tide.
Bring your attention to the very top of your head. Imagine a gentle warmth resting there, like sunlight on a quiet afternoon. And let that warmth begin to spread.
It flows down across your forehead, smoothing it. Down over your eyebrows. Around your eyes, which grow heavy and still.
It moves across your cheeks, and around your mouth. Your jaw loosens. Your lips part a little. Your tongue rests.
The warmth flows down the back of your head, and into your neck. Let your neck give its weight to the pillow. It has held your head up all day. It can rest now.
Now the warmth reaches your shoulders. Notice if they are holding anything. And let them drop. Let them spread out wide and soft against the bed.
It flows down into your upper arms, and they grow heavy. Down past your elbows, into your forearms. Into your wrists. Into your hands, and all the way out to the tips of your fingers.
Your arms are heavy and warm, resting by your sides. You could not lift them now if you tried, and you do not need to.
Bring your attention to your chest. Feel it rise as you breathe in, and fall as you breathe out. Let the warmth settle there, slow and steady.
Let it flow down into your stomach. Let your stomach go soft. There is nothing to hold in. Let it rise and fall with your breath.
Now feel your back against the bed. The upper back, between the shoulder blades. The middle of your back. The lower back. Let each part sink a little deeper into the mattress.
The warmth moves down into your hips, and they grow heavy and wide. Let them settle.
Down into your thighs. Long, heavy muscles, letting go of the day's walking and standing and sitting. Let them be completely still.
Into your knees. Into your calves, which soften, and grow warm. Into your ankles.
And at last, into your feet. The heels. The soles. Each toe, one by one, loose and warm.
Now your whole body is soft. From the top of your head, to the tips of your toes. Heavy, and warm, and supported.
Rest here for a while. Feel the whole of you, lying still in the dark, held by the bed.
If a part of you has tightened again, that is all right. Simply notice it, breathe into it, and let it soften once more.
With each breath out, you sink a little deeper. A little heavier. A little further from the day.
There is nothing more you need to do tonight. Your body knows how to sleep. Let it.
Rest now. Soft, and warm, and still.
Lie down in the way that feels most natural to you. On your back, or on your side, whichever your body prefers tonight. Let the bed take your weight.
This is a simple, old method for falling asleep quickly. You relax your body, one part at a time, and then you quiet your mind for a few slow breaths. That is all. There is nothing to get right.
Let your eyes close.
Begin with your face. Let your forehead go smooth, as if a warm hand has just rested there for a moment. Let your eyebrows drop.
Let the small muscles around your eyes go soft. Let your eyes sink back, heavy and still.
Now your jaw. Let your teeth part a little. Let your tongue rest loosely in your mouth, not touching the roof of it. Let your cheeks go slack.
Now let your shoulders drop. Further than you think they can. Let them fall away from your ears, down towards the bed.
Let your upper arms go heavy. Then your forearms. Then your hands. One side, and then the other. Let your fingers uncurl.
Breathe out slowly, and let your chest settle. Let it sink a little with the breath, and stay there.
Now your legs. Let your thighs go heavy, as if they were made of warm sand. Let your knees soften.
Let your calves relax. Then your ankles. Then your feet. Let your toes go loose.
Your whole body is heavy now. Heavy, and warm, and still. There is nothing it needs to hold.
Now, for the next few breaths, let your mind be just as still.
Picture yourself lying in a small boat on a calm lake, on a warm, clear night. Above you, nothing but a dark blue sky. The boat rocks very gently. There is nowhere to go.
If a thought comes, let it pass, like a ripple moving away across the water. And come back to the boat, and the sky, and the stillness.
Or, if it is easier, say three words quietly to yourself, over and over, slowly. Don't think. Don't think. Don't think.
Relax your face again. Let your shoulders drop again. Let your breath go long and slow.
The boat rocks gently. The night is warm and still.
Don't think. Just rest.
There is nothing more to do now. Let sleep come and find you.

This is yoga nidra, a practice of deep rest. Lie on your back if you can, arms a little away from your sides, palms facing up. Let your legs fall slightly apart. Make any small movement you need, and then let the body become still.

In yoga nidra, you do not need to try. You only listen to my voice, and follow it lightly, with your attention. If your mind wanders, that is fine. When you notice, simply come back to the voice. And if you fall asleep, that is fine too.
Let your eyes close. Take a slow breath in. And a long breath out.
Once more. Breathe in... and let it all go.
Become aware of the sounds around you. The farthest sound you can hear. Let it come, and let it go, without following it.
Now the sounds a little closer. Inside the room. And then the sound of your own breath.
Feel your body lying on the bed. The places where it touches the mattress. The back of the head. The shoulders. The back. The hips. The heels. Let all of them grow heavy.
Say to yourself, silently: I am awake, and I am aware. I am practising yoga nidra.
Now it is time for your intention. A short, simple sentence, said with feeling, as if it were already true. If you do not have one, you can use this one. I am at peace, and I sleep deeply.
Repeat your intention three times, silently, to yourself.
Now we will travel around the body. As I name each part, let your attention rest there for a moment, and then move on. There is nothing to do. Only notice.
The right hand. The right thumb. Second finger. Third finger. Fourth finger. The little finger. The palm of the hand. The back of the hand. The wrist.
The forearm. The elbow. The upper arm. The right shoulder. The right armpit. The right side of the waist. The right hip.
The right thigh. The knee. The calf. The ankle. The heel. The sole of the right foot. The top of the foot. The big toe. Second toe. Third toe. Fourth toe. The little toe.
Now the left hand. The left thumb. Second finger. Third finger. Fourth finger. The little finger. The palm of the hand. The back of the hand. The wrist.
The forearm. The elbow. The upper arm. The left shoulder. The left armpit. The left side of the waist. The left hip.
The left thigh. The knee. The calf. The ankle. The heel. The sole of the left foot. The top of the foot. The big toe. Second toe. Third toe. Fourth toe. The little toe.

Now the back of the body. The right shoulder blade. The left shoulder blade. The whole of the upper back. The lower back. The right buttock. The left buttock. The whole spine, from the base of the skull to the tailbone. Feel the whole back of the body, resting.

Now the top of the head. The forehead. The right eyebrow. The left eyebrow. The space between the eyebrows. The right eye. The left eye. The right ear. The left ear. The right cheek. The left cheek. The nose. The tip of the nose. The upper lip. The lower lip. The chin. The jaw. The throat.
The right side of the chest. The left side of the chest. The middle of the chest. The navel. The belly. The lower belly.
The whole right leg. The whole left leg. Both legs together.
The whole right arm. The whole left arm. Both arms together.
The whole back. The whole front of the body. The head. The whole body together. The whole body, lying still.
Now become aware of your breath. Do not change it. Simply watch the natural breath, flowing in, and flowing out.
Feel the breath at the belly. The belly rising as you breathe in... and falling as you breathe out.

Now we will count the breath, backwards, from twenty-seven down to one. Breathing in... twenty-seven. Breathing out... twenty-seven. Breathing in... twenty-six. Breathing out... twenty-six. Continue on your own, slowly, in your own time.
If you lose count, or make a mistake, simply begin again at twenty-seven. And if you reach one, let the counting go, and simply rest in the breath.
Let go of the counting now, wherever you are. Let the breath breathe itself.

Now we will awaken some feelings in the body. Become aware of heaviness. Feel the body becoming heavy. The arms heavy. The legs heavy. The head heavy, sinking into the pillow. The whole body so heavy, as if it were sinking down through the bed.
Now become aware of lightness. Feel the body becoming light. Light as a feather. So light that it could float up, above the bed. The whole body, light and weightless.
Now become aware of warmth. Remember the feeling of warmth. Sitting near a fire on a winter night. Warmth on the hands, on the face, through the whole body.
Now become aware of coolness. Remember the feeling of cool air. A cool breeze through an open window on a summer night. Cool on the skin, through the whole body.
Now let those feelings go. Let the body rest just as it is.
Now I will name some images. As you hear each one, let it appear in your mind, as clearly as it comes. Do not hold on to it. Let each image pass, and wait for the next.

A candle flame, very still... A quiet lake at night... The moon on the water... A lantern in a window... Snow falling slowly... A path through a pine forest... A cup of tea, steaming... Rain on a roof... A small boat, drifting...
A sleeping cat... Stars over the mountains... A warm blanket... A bird, folding its wings... Waves on the sand, coming and going... A door, gently closing... A dark, quiet sky...
Now let the images go. Become aware of the dark space in front of your closed eyes. Simply watch it, deep and soft, like the night sky.
Now remember your intention. The same sentence you chose at the beginning. Repeat it three times, silently, with feeling. Let it sink deep into the mind, like a seed into warm earth.
This practice of yoga nidra is now complete. But there is no need to come back. There is nowhere you need to be, and nothing more to do.
Let the body stay heavy and still. Let the breath stay slow. And let yourself drift, gently, all the way down, into sleep.
Sleep well.
